Table~\ref{tab:main} is the whole study on one page: six adaptations, eight models, and the three
regimes that separate them. Read down a block and the models agree with each other; read \emph{across}
the blocks and the bold moves. On stacks built from transforms the adapters were trained on, the best
arm is the KL-consistency arm on five models, the router system on two and breadth on one. On the held-out
family the router system takes six and the KL-consistency arm two; backwards the merge takes six. On the held-out family the bold moves to the router system on six of eight,
and on the reverse task to the merge on six --- both assembled from per-transform specialists. No arm wins everywhere, and the one that never loses is not the one that wins most often.


\subsection{Adaptation Succeeds on Seen Compositions}

Stacking is where adaptation was supposed to break, and it does not. Every arm roughly doubles the
untuned model on depth-2, -3 and -4 compositions of the seen transforms: 0.143 to 0.32--0.37 on
CodeLlama-7B, 0.161 to 0.39--0.45 on CodeLlama-34B, and so on down the panel. The spread among tuned
arms is three to six points, two to five times smaller than the gap to the untuned model, and a
single-adapter arm sits at the top of it on six of the eight models. Composition per se is not the difficulty: a model
that has seen identifier renaming and control-flow flattening separately handles them together.

This is the regime prior work reports, and if the evaluation stopped here the conclusion would be that
the choice of adaptation barely matters and the monolithic one is fine. The next two blocks are the
reason it does not stop here.


\subsection{Pooled Training Is the Worst Use of the Data on an Unseen Family}

The \emph{unseen family} block holds the held-out obfuscator and every stack containing it. No arm was
trained on it, and the ordering changes: breadth --- one adapter trained on the pooled data of all six
training conditions --- is below \emph{every} arm assembled from those same conditions' specialists,
on all eight models.

Paired by program with a cluster bootstrap over 2{,}000 resamples, and measured on the held-out family
itself, breadth is below the router system by 3.3--5.9 points on 8 of 8 models (significant on all 8), below
the merge by 2.3--5.2 on 8 of 8 (significant on 7), and below a LoRA trained on \emph{unobfuscated code
alone} by 2.7--4.7 on 8 of 8 (significant on 6).

Measured over the whole block --- the family plus the six stacks that contain it --- the same orderings
hold but the margins shrink: breadth is below the router system on 8 of 8 (significant on all 8, 2.5--4.6
points), below the merge on 7 of 8 (significant on 5, 1.8--3.0), and below clean-code tuning on 7 of 8
but significantly on only 2 (1.3--1.6). The dilution is itself informative. A stack that contains the
unseen family also contains transforms breadth was trained on, and breadth handles those well; its
deficit is concentrated where the input is purely unfamiliar and fades as the familiar returns. That is
what memorising a transform looks like, and it is not what an invariance would predict.

The merge comparison is exactly data-matched: its six ingredient adapters are trained on precisely the
six conditions breadth pools, at the same rank, from the same base model, so the only difference is
whether those rows were learned in one set of weights or in six that are then composed. The router system is
\emph{not} data-matched --- it carries two further specialists, on the transforms \texttt{S3} and
\texttt{S4}, that neither breadth nor the merge is trained on. Its advantage does not come from them:
measured against the merge, it is at least as large on composites that contain neither \texttt{S3} nor
\texttt{S4} ($+2.8$ to $+5.3$) as on those that do ($+2.2$ to $+4.7$), on all eight models. We
nonetheless treat the exactly-matched merge comparison as the load-bearing one.

An adapter that has never seen an obfuscated program generalises
better to an unseen obfuscator than one trained on five of them. Training on more transforms made the
model worse at a transform it had not seen --- which is what transform memorisation predicts and what
invariance would forbid.


\subsection{Single Adapters Lose the Untrained Direction}

The backward task asks for a call that produces a given return value, on the same programs. No arm is
trained in this direction, so it measures what adaptation did to program understanding rather than to
task fitting.

Every single-adapter arm goes red somewhere in the backward block, and the pattern is systematic
rather than model-specific. Pooling every backward condition that clears the format gate and pairing by
program, clean-code tuning is below the untuned model on six of eight models (significantly on four),
breadth on four of the six where it is readable (significantly on four), and the KL-consistency arm on
six (significantly on five, by as much as 13.2 points on Granite-3.1-8B). The merges are the exception:
DARE-TIES is \emph{above} the untuned model on seven of eight models ($+3.0$ to $+6.4$ points,
significant on all seven) and null on the eighth. It is not significantly below the untuned model on
any model in any of the three blocks. On that eighth model, Granite-3.1-8B, replacing the random drop
of Eq.~\ref{eq:dare} with a magnitude trim recovers a significant gain, which localises the null to
the sparsification step rather than to merging (Appendix~\ref{app:mergevariants}). The arm that wins the seen-stack block is the clearest loser here.

Two qualifications belong with that result rather than in a footnote. Backward is graded by execution
--- any call returning the gold value counts, because inversion is many-to-one --- and 15\,\% of items
have a trivial gold ($0$, \texttt{None}, \texttt{[]}, \ldots) that a well-formed guess can hit. On
Llama-3.1-8B, whose untuned backward score is the panel's second highest, that accounts for nearly all
of its lead: by exact-argument recovery it is 0.086 against CodeLlama-7B's 0.084, the same model. The
merge's advantage survives the stricter grade on that model; some other differences do not, and we
report both gradings in Appendix~\ref{app:absmaster}.


\subsection{Direction Locking Explains the Backward Failures}

The backward failures are not parse failures. When a single-adapter arm is asked for an input and
produces something ungradable, the reply is most often \emph{exactly the gold forward answer} --- the
return value of the program, correctly computed, in answer to a question that asked for something else.
The arm did not lose the ability to read the program; it lost the ability to be asked a different
question about it.

Measured as the share of backward replies that are exactly the gold forward answer, the untuned models
sit at the floor (0.000--0.056) and so do both merges (0.000--0.002 across all eight models). Every
single-adapter arm is above that floor on every model but one --- the exception is clean-code tuning on
Llama-3.1-8B, at 0.001 --- and the panel maximum --- 0.680, on CodeGemma-7B
--- belongs to the KL-consistency arm, which also holds the per-model maximum on five of the eight. Its
extra loss term is a KL divergence to a clean-code teacher's answer-token distribution: the arm that
most explicitly optimises for producing the forward answer is the arm that most often produces it when
asked for something else.

This connects the two out-of-distribution blocks. Monolithic training fits the task as it was posed:
these transforms, this direction. Composing separately-trained specialists in weight space does not
produce that fit, which is why the merge gives up three to six points where the fit pays and keeps its
competence where the fit does not transfer.
